title: Ki Tisa: the half shekel (Exodus 30:11–16)
hook: rich and poor give the same half coin; no one counts as whole alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold plate engraved holy to the Lord, worn where the priest himself could never read it. Your line was holy on the forehead. What word did you wear? Today, a new portion. Day three hundred sixty-three.

A census sounds like the dullest thing in the world. Forms, clipboards, a knock on the door. But in the Torah, a head count carries a danger: the text warns of a plague coming with the counting. So when Moses is told to count the Israelites, he's told not to count heads at all. Count coins. Each one counted, from twenty years old and up, brings one coin, and the coins are counted instead. Here's the twist. The coin isn't a whole one. It's half. And the price is fixed. The richest family in the camp and the poorest one hand over exactly the same thing. Today we open a new portion, Ki Tisa, with half a coin.
screen: `COUNT COINS, NOT HEADS.` → `EVERYONE BRINGS HALF.` → `RICH AND POOR, THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Ki tisa means when you lift up, and the full phrase is when you lift up the head of the children of Israel: an old way of saying, when you take a count. The idiom is lovely. To count someone is to lift their head. Then the instruction: each one gives half a shekel, an offering to the Lord, and the text adds a line worth hearing slowly. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel." Think about how unusual that is. Plenty of gifts are measured by what you can afford. This one isn't. Nobody can buy a bigger share of the count. Nobody is left out for lack of money. The silver went to the service of the tent of meeting, and the text calls it a ransom for the soul, a covering, so that no plague would come with the counting. Rashi passes on a midrash: Moses couldn't picture the coin, so God showed him a coin made of fire and said, like this. And why half? The Torah doesn't say. Commentators have offered answers, and one you'll hear is simple: no one is complete alone. You bring your half, someone else brings theirs, and only together does anything add up. Jews still remember the half shekel. On a Shabbat just before the month of Adar, the passage is read aloud, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local money to charity.
screen: `KI TISA: WHEN YOU LIFT THE HEAD.` · `NO MORE, NO LESS THAN HALF.` · `A COIN OF FIRE.` · `NO ONE IS COMPLETE ALONE.` · then, large: `HALF MAKES A WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add your half to something shared. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're part of: a family, a team, a street, a group chat, a congregation. Where is it waiting on your half? A dish washed, a message answered, a coin in a jar, ten minutes of help. Don't measure it against what anyone else gives. Just see it clearly, and decide when you'll bring it. Then sit with the picture of everyone's halves adding up. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tisa. When you lift up: the portion that opens with a census counted in half coins, the same from rich and poor.
Your line: half makes a whole. Today, add one small thing to something shared, and let it be enough that it's your half. Day three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: The half-shekel passage is read as Parashat Shekalim on the Shabbat before Adar, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local currency to charity in its memory.

original.note: Hebrew: the half shekel, the coin every adult brought to be counted.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient tax.
what it means: a census counted in half coins, the same for everyone, so no one's share is bigger and no one is a number.
what a scholar hears: ki tisa et rosh, lift up the head, is the Hebrew idiom for taking a count; Rashi on 30:13 cites the midrash of the coin of fire.

sources.quoted: The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel

sources.ref: Mishnah Shekalim 1:1; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 694:1 (Rema)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'counting treats people as numbers' replaced by the text's own reason (no plague, 30:12); cut 'quoted ever since', 'almost every gift', 'for centuries' and 'best known'; Purim half-coin custom no longer claimed for 'many'; Shekalim is 'the passage', not the portion.
Exodus 30:15 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Counting by coins because a direct census brings danger (30:12, 'that there be no plague among them'): confirm framing.
Rashi on 30:13: God showed Moses a coin of fire (from Tanchuma); confirm.
'No one is complete alone' is offered as one commentators' reading, not the Torah's stated reason; confirm attribution is fair (it appears in various later homilies).
Custom of giving three half coins before Purim (Rema, OC 694:1): confirm; some give on the Fast of Esther.
Parashat Shekalim is read on the Shabbat before Rosh Chodesh Adar (or on it); confirm wording.
